name: Dish Shopping
description: There are $$$m$$$ people living in a city. There are $$$n$$$ dishes sold in the city. Each dish $$$i$$$ has a price $$$p_i$$$, a standard $$$s_i$$$ and a beauty $$$b_i$$$. Each person $$$j$$$ has an income of $$$inc_j$$$ and a preferred beauty $$$pref_j$$$. A person would never buy a dish whose standard is less than the person's income. Also, a person can't afford a dish with a price greater than the income of the person. In other words, a person $$$j$$$ can buy a dish $$$i$$$ only if $$$p_i \leq inc_j \leq s_i$$$. Also, a person $$$j$$$ can buy a dish $$$i$$$, only if $$$|b_i-pref_j| \leq (inc_j-p_i)$$$. In other words, if the price of the dish is less than the person's income by $$$k$$$, the person will only allow the absolute difference of at most $$$k$$$ between the beauty of the dish and his/her preferred beauty. Print the number of dishes that can be bought by each person in the city.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$, $$$1 \leq m \leq 10^5$$$), the number of dishes available in the city and the number of people living in the city. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_i \leq 10^9$$$), the price of each dish. The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq s_i \leq 10^9$$$), the standard of each dish. The fourth line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq b_i \leq 10^9$$$), the beauty of each dish. The fifth line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$inc_j$$$ ($$$1 \leq inc_j \leq 10^9$$$), the income of every person. The sixth line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$pref_j$$$ ($$$1 \leq pref_j \leq 10^9$$$), the preferred beauty of every person. It is guaranteed that for all integers $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, the following condition holds: $$$p_i \leq s_i$$$.
output_specification: Print $$$m$$$ integers, the number of dishes that can be bought by every person living in the city.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1139F — Dish Shopping [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
